newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-One-off measures insufficient for EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-One-off measures insufficient for EMU.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer warned European countries on Wednesday that one-off measures by European nations to reduce budget deficits would not be enough to allow them to join a single European currency in 1999.
In an interview with the French daily Le Monde, he said Europe would have to look at long-term prospects when it decided in early 1998 which nations could join the EU's economic union.
"One-off results are not enough as proof of respect for the stability criteria," he said.
"All the figures, for example the budget figures, must be fulfilled not on the basis of a massaging of the balance sheet, but in the direction of long-term solidity," he said.

He declined to say which countries would join in 1999, but said Italy, which plans a special one-off euro tax to reduce its budget deficit in time to qualify, would be welcome -- provided it could keep up its efforts afterwards.
"If Italy fulfils the criteria in a lasting way it will of course be welcome in the community of the euro," he said.

Various countries have been accused by economists of window-dressing to meet a Maastricht Treaty requirement to cut budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997, the year on which eligibility for membership will be judged.
France set the tone last month with a budget which relies on money for pensions being transferred from state-owned France Telecom to the state to meet the three percent target.
Asked whether he considered this window-dressing, Tietmeyer said he had no intention of criticising countries by name.
But he noted it was France which proposed the three percent figure, and this had been agreed by its partners in the 15-nation bloc.
"I have the impression that some people do not like to be reminded of something to which they have already given their agreement," he said.
Economists say there is no question of launching a single currency without France, but they say its action will make it harder to exclude others which resort to similar measures.
Tietmeyer also said a budget stability pact limiting budget deficits after monetary union was important to ensure that all countries shared a common culture of supporting stability.
"For a long time to come, we will have to live in Europe without a common political will, an element which has, however, accompanied the launch of any single currency.
"We will continue to live in national states. That is why it is so important to have the same culture of stability," he said.
Monetary union must be a success, but it must also be accepted by everybody in all its political implications.
"Without that, there would be a very brutal reversal in European integration," he said.
He also warned there should be no illusions the single currency, the euro, would help create jobs without needed labour market reforms.
"On the contrary, the euro will increase competition between countries and markets and abolish the exchange rate tool, which could be used up to now as an 'airbag'," he said.
But he said he believed monetary union would start on time in 1999, barring surprises between now and then.
"There are strong reasons to believe today that the timetable will be respected, at least by a limited number of countries, as foreseen in the Maastricht Treaty.
"I start from the principle that if nothing surprising happens between now and then, monetary union will begin at the start of 1999."
He added he wanted a "strong and stable" euro and said the exchange rates of many European currencies against the dollar were more realistic now than a short time ago.
He was also happy with the mark's rate within the European Monetary System (EMS). "I have no problems with the current rate of the mark within the EMS, which is, basically, correct."
He said he was unable to tell if there was room to lower interest rates in Germany, but said economic growth was not handicapped by monetary policy.
"We do not start from the principle that we will have to raise rates in the near term. I cannot, however, say if there is still a little room to go lower," he said.
